**Greedy decoding repeatedly follows the locally most likely continuation.** If the generated phrase makes repeating that phrase even more likely, the model can enter a self-reinforcing loop. Low temperature sharpens the same preference and may reduce opportunities to escape it. [1](https://arxiv.org/abs/2211.17192)

A repetition penalty lowers scores for previously generated tokens. This can discourage loops, but repeated tokens are sometimes necessary in code, names, lists, or exact quotations. Penalizing them indiscriminately can damage the answer.

**Min-p sampling uses a relative probability cutoff.** If the most probable token has probability 0.5 and min-p is 0.1, keep tokens with probability at least 0.05, then renormalize. The threshold adapts to how peaked the distribution is. If only the loop token survives, min-p does not solve the loop.

Neither technique guarantees factuality or nonrepetition. Compare decoding settings on realistic prompts, and inspect training-data or model issues if repetition is systematic. A sampling control changes how the model's distribution is used; it does not necessarily repair the distribution itself.

**Technical details and references.**

Greedy decoding repeatedly chooses the highest conditional probability and can enter self-reinforcing loops under the model's learned distribution. Low temperature sharpens that preference. Repetition penalties reduce scores of previously used tokens; min-p sampling retains tokens whose probability exceeds a fraction of the current maximum. [1](https://arxiv.org/abs/2211.17192)

$$A=\{i:p_i\ge p_{min}\max_jp_j\}.$$

Neither guarantees no repetition or factuality. Penalizing repeated tokens can damage names, code, or legitimate repeated phrases; min-p may retain only the dominant loop token if the distribution is very peaked. Evaluate task-specific decoding and consider model/data issues rather than treating a sampling knob as a universal cure.
